chapters.title: Chapter 1: Real Estate Through an Investor's Eyes

lessons.title: The Indian Property Market: Cities, Cycles and Who Drives Demand

children.text: In 2025, housing sales across India's top seven cities fell 14% by number of homes, according to ANAROCK. In the same year, the total value of those sales rose 6%, to over ₹6 lakh crore. Fewer homes, more money. If you can explain that contradiction, you already understand more about the Indian property market than most people buying in it. By the end of this lesson, you will.

body.text: There is no single "Indian property market." There are hundreds of micro-markets, each moved by three forces: jobs, infrastructure and credit. Follow those three and you can read almost any headline about real estate.

children.text: Where the Homes Are Being Sold

markDefs.definition: The seven largest residential markets tracked by most Indian property research firms: Mumbai Metropolitan Region, Delhi-NCR, Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad, Chennai and Kolkata.

children.text: Most national property data you will read covers the
top seven cities
. They are not the whole country, but they are where most organised developer sales, home loans and price data are concentrated.

body.caption: Housing sales in the top seven cities, 2025 (ANAROCK)

cells: IT services and global capability centres

body.title: Share of 2025 housing sales by city (units)
The western dominance
body.prompt: Mumbai sold 1,27,875 homes and Pune sold 65,135 in 2025, out of 3,95,625 across the top seven cities. What share of all sales did these two western markets make up, in %? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: 1,27,875 + 65,135 = 1,93,010. 1,93,010 ÷ 3,95,625 = 0.488, or about 49%. Nearly one in every two homes sold in India's big seven cities was in Maharashtra's two largest markets.

children.text: Solving the Puzzle: Fewer Homes, More Money

markDefs.definition: A shift in sales towards larger, more expensive homes, so the average price per home sold rises even when the number of homes sold falls.

children.text: The answer to the opening puzzle is
premiumisation

. Developers have been launching more homes priced above ₹1 crore, and affluent buyers have been buying them. Meanwhile, affordable housing under ₹50 lakh has seen fewer launches, as land and construction costs make it harder for developers to earn a margin. The result: fewer homes sold, but each one sold for much more.

body.title: Average ticket size
body.prompt: Top seven city housing sales were worth about ₹6 lakh crore in 2025, across 3,95,625 homes. What was the average value per home sold, in ₹ crore? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: ₹6,00,000 crore ÷ 3,95,625 = ₹1.52 crore per home. In 2024, sales of about ₹5.68 lakh crore across 4,59,645 homes worked out to about ₹1.24 crore. The average home sold became roughly 23% more expensive in a single year.

body.text: Premiumisation matters for investors in two ways. First, the average buyer in the top seven cities is now spending well over ₹1 crore, which keeps many first-time buyers renting for longer and supports rental demand. Second, when too many luxury homes are launched at once, unsold stock piles up at the top end. Knight Frank reported that unsold inventory in the ₹2 to 5 crore band jumped 43% year on year in H1 2026.

children.text: Who Actually Drives Demand
End-users.
Families buying a home to live in. They are the backbone of the market, and they buy based on salaries, EMIs and life events like marriage and children.
Investors.
Buyers chasing rent or price gains, often in under-construction projects. They amplify booms and are the first to disappear in slowdowns.
NRIs.
Non-resident Indians in the Gulf, US, UK and Singapore buying back home, especially in Kerala, Punjab, Hyderabad and Bengaluru. A weaker rupee makes Indian property cheaper for them.

markDefs.definition: An offshore office set up by a multinational company to run technology, finance, analytics, research or operations work for its global business.

children.text: Corporates.
Companies leasing offices, warehouses and data centres. The biggest force here is the
global capability centre (GCC)
, the Indian back offices and tech hubs of firms like JPMorgan, Walmart and Target.
Government.
Through infrastructure like metros, expressways and airports, housing schemes like PMAY, and policy levers like stamp duty rates and RERA.

children.text: The Jobs-to-Homes Chain
Residential demand rarely starts with homes. It starts with offices. Here is how a single GCC lease in Hyderabad's HITEC City ripples outward:
Office leased.
A global bank signs for 5 lakh sq ft of office space.
Hiring.
At roughly 100 to 150 sq ft per seat, that is space for several thousand well-paid employees, many relocating from other cities.
Rental demand.
New joiners rent first, pushing up rents in Gachibowli, Kondapur and Narsingi.
Home purchases.
After two to four years, many of them buy, using home loans backed by stable salaries.
Everything else follows.
Malls, schools, hospitals and restaurants open nearby, which makes the area more desirable and supports prices further.

body.title: Seats from square feet
body.prompt: A GCC leases 5,00,000 sq ft of office space. If each employee needs about 125 sq ft including shared areas, roughly how many employees can the space hold?
body.explanation: 5,00,000 ÷ 125 = 4,000 seats. Four thousand salaried professionals, most earning well above the city average, is a substantial source of rental and purchase demand for nearby neighbourhoods.

children.text: Property Moves in Cycles

Real estate does not rise in a straight line. Because a project takes three to five years from launch to delivery, supply always reacts late to demand. Developers launch aggressively when sales are strong, and those homes arrive just as demand cools. That lag creates a cycle with four recognisable phases.

body.caption: The four phases of a property cycle

cells: Sales pick up, unsold stock starts falling, few new launches
2021, as low home loan rates pulled buyers back after COVID
Strong sales, rising rents, developers launch heavily
2022 to 2024, with record sales in the top seven cities
Launches outpace sales, unsold inventory builds, offers and discounts appear
2025 into 2026, with falling volumes and rising luxury inventory
Sales slump, projects stall, weak developers default
Flat or falling in real terms

Two Decades of Indian Property Cycles

events.title: The first big boom
events.description: Cheap credit, IT hiring and investor speculation push prices up sharply across metros.

events.title: Global financial crisis
events.description: Sales freeze, developers cut prices and launch smaller, cheaper homes to survive.

events.title: Launch frenzy
events.description: Developers launch heavily, often using buyer advances to fund new land purchases.

events.title: The long slump
events.description: Unsold inventory, demonetisation, the NBFC crisis and stalled projects keep prices flat in many cities for years.

events.title: Post-COVID upcycle
events.description: Low interest rates and demand for bigger homes drive record sales, led by listed developers.

events.title: Volumes cool, prices hold
events.description: Sales volumes fall, luxury inventory rises, and buyers regain some negotiating power.

children.text: Reading the Market's Pulse

markDefs.definition: The number of months it would take to sell all currently unsold homes at the current pace of sales, assuming no new launches.

children.text: The single most useful number for judging where a city sits in its cycle is
months of inventory
, sometimes called the inventory overhang. Property research firms like ANAROCK, Knight Frank and PropEquity publish it for major cities every quarter.

body.caption: Lower means a tighter market that favours sellers. Higher means more choice and bargaining power for buyers.

body.title: How long to clear the stock?
body.prompt: A city has 90,000 unsold homes and sells an average of 4,500 homes a month. How many months of inventory does it have?
body.explanation: 90,000 ÷ 4,500 = 20 months. As a broad rule of thumb, readings well below 18 to 24 months suggest a tight market, while readings climbing well above that suggest oversupply and more room to negotiate.

body.caption: Five signals worth tracking every quarter

cells: Sales keep pace with or exceed launches
Rising roughly with or above prices
Prices rising far faster than rents
Heavy discounts, subvention schemes, "no EMI till possession" offers

body.text: National and city headlines average out wildly different micro-markets. A city can report rising unsold stock while one well-connected suburb near a new metro line is selling out. RBI data for early 2026 showed house price growth being led by cities like Nagpur, Chandigarh and Jaipur, not the metros that dominate the news. Always drill down to the micro-market you are actually buying in.

body.label: India's official urban housing shortage estimate
body.context: From a government technical group estimate for 2012. More than 95% of the shortage was in homes for economically weaker and lower-income groups, the segment developers find hardest to build profitably. A national shortage does not mean every ₹2 crore flat will find a buyer.

body.title: Spot the phase
body.question: In a city, new launches have exceeded sales for four straight quarters, unsold inventory is rising, and developers are advertising "pay 20% now, rest on possession" offers. Which phase of the cycle does this most likely signal?
body.explanation: Launches outpacing sales, rising inventory and aggressive payment offers are classic hypersupply signs. Developers are competing for fewer buyers, which usually means slower price growth and better bargaining power for buyers.

body.title: Name the demand driver
body.textWithBlank: A GCC, the Indian tech or operations hub of a multinational company, stands for Global ___ Centre.
body.explanation: Global Capability Centres took nearly 40% of India's office leasing in 2025 and are one of the biggest drivers of housing demand in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune.

body.title: The broker's urgency pitch
body.scenario: Karan, a 40-year-old business owner in Delhi, is being shown a ₹2.8 crore under-construction flat on Dwarka Expressway, Gurugram. The broker says: "Prices here are up 20% in a year. Luxury is the only segment growing. Book this week before the next price hike."
body.prompt: Using what you learned about demand drivers and cycles, what should Karan check before deciding?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Cycle position: a 20% one-year jump often happens late in an expansion. Karan should check whether launches in the area are outpacing sales.
2. Inventory: Knight Frank reported unsold stock in the ₹2 to 5 crore band rose 43% year on year in H1 2026. Is this micro-market adding to that pile?
3. Who is buying: are recent buyers end-users moving in, or investors hoping to flip before possession? Investor-heavy projects are more fragile in a slowdown.
4. Jobs and infrastructure: what employment hubs and completed infrastructure actually support demand here, versus promised projects?
5. Rents: what would this flat rent for today? If the rental yield is very low, the price depends entirely on future appreciation.
6. Urgency: "book this week" is a sales tactic. In a market with rising luxury inventory, the buyer usually has more time and more bargaining power, not less.

body.title: Researching a Micro-Market
steps: Identify the three largest employers or job hubs within a 30-minute commute
List infrastructure that is completed, not just announced
Find the latest launches vs sales trend for the city from ANAROCK, Knight Frank or PropEquity
Check current rents for similar flats on MagicBricks or 99acres
Compare asking prices with recent registered transaction prices where available
Note any discounts or payment schemes developers are offering nearby

A shift in sales towards more expensive homes, so average ticket sizes rise even when unit sales fall.
Global Capability Centre: an Indian office of a multinational that runs tech, finance or operations work for the global business.
Unsold homes divided by average monthly sales. Higher means oversupply and more buyer bargaining power.
The cycle phase where launches outpace sales and unsold stock builds, slowing price growth.
MMR, Delhi-NCR, Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad, Chennai and Kolkata: the markets most research covers.

points: India's property market is really hundreds of micro-markets, moved by jobs, infrastructure and credit.
In 2025, top seven city sales fell 14% by volume but rose 6% by value, as premiumisation lifted the average ticket to about ₹1.52 crore.
Mumbai and Pune together made up about 49% of 2025 sales in the top seven cities.
Office leasing, led by GCCs, feeds rental demand first and home purchases later.
Because supply lags demand by years, property moves through recovery, expansion, hypersupply and recession.
Track launches vs sales, months of inventory, rents, loan rates and developer offers to judge where a market sits in its cycle.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Market data comes from third-party research firms, whose methods and city definitions differ, and conditions can change quickly. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
